title: Rare Scenarios Have Poor Interaction Support
excerpt: Rare scenarios have poor interaction support when software gives high-quality support to the main workflow but weak guidance, feedback, and recovery to non-standard operational states. The failure often appears when development assumptions define what is rare instead of observed operational reality.
metaDescription: Defines the failure pattern where non-standard operational scenarios are treated as edge cases and receive weak guidance, feedback, and recovery support.
summary: This failure pattern concerns uneven interaction quality between the designed path and the scenarios that fall outside it. It is especially consequential when scenarios treated as edge cases during design are common in real operation.
definition: Rare scenarios have poor interaction support when non-standard operational scenarios receive generic, incomplete, or weak interface support because they were treated as edge cases rather than first-class design requirements.
keyFacts: The failure is the structural treatment of non-standard scenarios as design afterthoughts.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Rare scenarios have poor interaction support when a software system is smooth on the main workflow but rough, confusing, or unusable when users reach scenarios the design team treated as edge cases. The failure is not only the presence of errors. The failure is the gap between interaction quality on the designed path and interaction quality off it.

This failure often appears because the development team's model of normal use differs from operational reality. Clean data, ideal workflows, standard demonstrations, and predictable state transitions may define the designed path. Real use may involve messy data, sensor faults, peak-load conditions, missing integration signals, interrupted workflows, or unresolved command outcomes.

When rare scenarios receive poor interaction support, users may reach a dead end. The interface may provide no guidance, no useful error communication, and no recovery path. In those conditions, a technically detectable state is still operationally unsupported.

## Failure pattern: non-standard scenarios are treated as design afterthoughts

Rare-scenario support fails when non-standard scenarios are added later, tested less thoroughly, and handled defensively rather than designed as operational states. The result is a system whose interaction quality is uneven: refined on the workflow the design team expected, weak on the workflows that users actually encounter under real conditions.

The failure is distinct from interfaces that make errors easy to commit during normal operation. Error prevention in normal use concerns the conditions that lead users into mistakes on the main path. Rare-scenario support concerns the quality of guidance, feedback, and recovery when the user is no longer on that main path.

The failure is also distinct from a system that fights the user's task model. A system can have a well-aligned primary workflow and still fail when operationally common exceptions, degraded states, or ambiguous outcomes are not given specific interaction support.

## Mechanism: the happy-path model excludes operationally common scenarios

The most consequential mechanism is a narrow definition of normal use. A product team may design around clean data, standard workflows, and ideal conditions because those are the scenarios available in training material, demonstration datasets, and internal testing.

The missing input is empirical knowledge about operational reality. Users may first encounter the system with data, conditions, and constraints that the demonstration never included. If those conditions were not present during domain learning, they are not treated as design requirements. They are not necessarily designed against; they are absent from the design process.

Polymatica illustrates this mechanism. Training used clean, structurally ideal data. First independent use involved users importing their own real datasets, which contained inconsistent columns, mixed entity types, and values that did not match the apparent structure. The interface showed the data but did not provide a data preparation step, a preview, or guidance on how the data should be structured for the intended OLAP operations.

## Mechanism: rare is defined by development assumptions rather than operational frequency

Rare-scenario support fails when rarity is assigned from the development team's assumptions rather than observed operational frequency. A scenario can be unusual in a test dataset and common in deployment.

Triopsis illustrates this mechanism. Weather incidents, equipment unavailability, crew shortages, and routing conflicts were treated as exceptions in the interface. In utilities and road maintenance operations, those conditions were part of the daily work of scheduling. The interface was navigable under normal conditions, but three in-situ observation sessions targeting peak-load, concurrent-exception conditions documented a large interaction quality gap.

The same mechanism can apply to sensor-driven systems. Delayed sensor readings, contradictory readings, and calibration faults can occur as known conditions in real building installations. If these states are treated as exceptional failures rather than operational states, the interface may communicate that something is wrong without communicating what it means or what the user should do.

## Mechanism: generic error handling replaces specific operational states

Generic error handling is often the default outcome when unusual states are treated as exceptions to manage rather than as operational states to communicate. A sensor fault may produce an error dialogue. A data inconsistency may trigger a generic error message. A configuration conflict may generate a warning.

These responses can be technically accurate and operationally unhelpful. They communicate that the state is not normal, but they do not communicate what has happened, what it means for the current task, or what path is available next.

The design problem is the minimum-viable quality of communication at the moment users need the highest-quality support. A user in a non-standard scenario usually needs clearer state naming, stronger orientation, and more specific recovery guidance than a user following the standard workflow.

## Polymatica: messy real-world data was the common first-use scenario

Polymatica's GPU-backed OLAP analytics engine had a large gap between the training scenario and first independent use. Training used clean datasets whose columns contained what their names implied and whose formats matched system expectations. First independent use involved users importing their own datasets, which were messy, inconsistent, and structurally varied.

The dead end appeared when users could not identify which column to perform operations on. The interface showed the data, but it did not help users understand why the data produced unexpected results, what was inconsistent in it, or what had to change to make the intended operation possible.

Before the redesign, 2% of users could complete key operations independently. The messy-data scenario was not a rare edge case measured by that figure. It was the standard condition of real operational data that the 2% figure exposed as poorly supported.

After the redesign introduced a data preparation and preview step, users could inspect data before committing to operations, identify structural issues, and rename or exclude columns. The messy-data failure mode largely disappeared from support requests. Independent task completion rose to 40% after release 1 and 56% after release 2, measured through product analytics in the live system.

## Triopsis: daily scheduling exceptions needed first-class workflow states

Triopsis served schedulers whose operating environment regularly included weather incidents, equipment failures, crew shortages, and job conflicts. These were not exceptional in practice. They were the daily material of scheduling work in utilities and road maintenance operations.

The previous interface was designed around a normal schedule in which jobs were assigned, resources were available, and the plan executed as written. Exception conditions were detectable by the system, but they were not first-class interface states with dedicated interaction paths. Schedulers had to manage exception conditions through the same interface used for the non-exceptional case.

The redesign treated exception conditions as first-class operational states. Predictive conflict indicators surfaced exception conditions before they became committed states requiring reversal. Dedicated action paths addressed weather incidents, partial completions, and equipment conflicts directly rather than routing them through workflows designed for the normal case.

Measured in the live product through product analytics, Triopsis recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning. The available case evidence connects the 62% faster job discovery result most directly to exception-specific interaction support, because first-class exception states reduced the scanning and navigation effort required to identify and act on them.

## Elsner Cala Touch KNX: sensor faults were designed as named states

Elsner Cala Touch KNX receives inputs from multiple sensors, including weather stations, CO2 probes, humidity sensors, temperature probes, and the main heating unit. Real building installations include delayed readings from high-latency sensors, contradictory readings from sensors out of calibration with each other, and calibration faults in individual sensors.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated these conditions as named, specific interface states rather than generic error conditions. A delayed reading was displayed as a pending reading, making clear that no action was required. A contradictory reading identified the contradiction. A calibration fault was surfaced as a specific, actionable state rather than through generic error handling.

The alert hierarchy also distinguished signal priority. Heating unit alerts were treated as primary signals in the visual hierarchy. Minor notifications such as open window detection were treated as visually secondary. This prevented every sensor condition from making an equal demand on user attention.

Sensor fault handling and firmware-aligned behaviour were confirmed in prototype testing with Elsner's engineers. A formal usability test with 12 subjects confirmed that navigation and temperature comprehension met the requirements of the interface under the conditions of use. The available evidence does not provide independently quantified post-deployment measurement for this sensor-fault handling.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses rare-scenario support

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses rare-scenario support by discovering what rare means operationally before design decisions are made. The method treats non-standard scenarios as first-class design requirements when operational reality shows that users will encounter them.

Domain learning is the prerequisite. In the Polymatica engagement, Creative Navy ran the system against real internal datasets during the research phase. The messy-data failure appeared because real data was used, which made the failure diagnosable as a design requirement rather than as user error.

In the Triopsis engagement, Creative Navy used three in-situ observation sessions that explicitly targeted peak-load, concurrent-exception conditions. The research programme was designed to find what operational reality looked like outside the happy path rather than to confirm that the happy path was well supported.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method then refuses the edge case as a design category when a scenario is operationally meaningful. In the Elsner engagement, sensor fault conditions were designed explicitly from the start of the Iterative System Building phase. In the Triopsis engagement, exception conditions were built as first-class workflow states with dedicated interaction paths before the redesign was considered complete.

## Evidence from Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and KISPE Space

Raymarine's partner brief named the operating condition at the centre of this failure pattern: a critical action may occur after months without using the relevant function. For a fixed-mount VHF radio, distress and safety functions may be precisely the functions an operator has not touched since the radio was installed.

In UX development for Raymarine, safety, degradation, and integration were addressed as a dedicated sprint. Outgoing distress, received distress, and locally initiated man overboard were specified as three different workflows. Four priority levels were constructed with cross-state rules. Forty-three exception cases were documented with feedback, action constraints, and recovery. Twenty-eight functions were assigned to the radio, the chartplotter, or a shared information boundary. Handover preparation consolidated 32 UX decisions and defined 23 screen families and 18 component requirements.

Raymarine's degraded conditions were enumerated rather than generalised. The exception catalogue contained 43 exception records across eight independent state axes: voice radio state, display context, calling transaction, AIS data quality, positioning, safety incident, interruption, and chartplotter link. The governing design statement was that a current screen is not a system state, and that the interface is a state interpreter rather than the source of truth for radio outcomes. The catalogue was partly evaluated: interruption, position, receiver, and connectivity cases were put to operators on a bench; the other thirty-odd cases were not.

Schone Airspace Group provides a different evidential class. A rare scenario involving a command whose outcome cannot be established was designed as a named operational state. A response window that elapsed without a conclusive event produced an explicit unknown state retaining the target, the action, and the request identifier, with no automatic retry. The accepted cost was that unknown is less reassuring than a binary outcome, but it is accurate and supports a deliberate subsequent check. The product was built and is in test; this is a designed state, not an operational deployment claim.

KISPE Space provides another evidential class. The engagement documented 40 edge cases and degraded states with 12 annotated plates. Each case specified the input condition, the visible response, the recovery path, the misinterpretation it prevents, and a verification that would expose a dangerous misunderstanding. The verification vocabulary is specification language, not executed testing. The catalogue was specified against a synthetic fixture and never exercised against a running system. The product was built, but Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

## Boundaries and limits

Rare-scenario support is not the same as preventing ordinary user errors. A normal workflow can make errors easy to commit, and that is a separate error-and-recovery failure. Rare-scenario support concerns what happens when the user reaches a path that received thin design coverage.

Rare-scenario support is also not identical to task-model misalignment. A product may support the main task model well and still fail when degraded states, exceptions, or ambiguous outcomes are not supported explicitly.

The evidence examples have different strengths and should not be blended. Polymatica and Triopsis include product analytics from live systems. Elsner includes prototype testing with engineers and a formal usability test with 12 subjects, but not independently quantified post-deployment measurement for the sensor-fault behaviour. Raymarine's exception catalogue was partly evaluated on a bench. Schone Airspace Group's unknown state is a designed state in a product that is in test. KISPE Space's edge-case catalogue specified verification checks that were not executed.

## Related pages

Errors Are Easy To Make is the adjacent failure concerned with interface conditions that make errors easy to commit during normal operation. Rare Scenarios Have Poor Interaction Support concerns the quality of support when the user is no longer on the normal path.

The System Fights The User Task is the adjacent workflow failure concerned with a fundamental mismatch between the system's task model and the user's task model. Rare-scenario support can fail even when the primary task model is aligned.

The Triopsis, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, and KISPE Space case pages provide related evidence for exception handling, degraded conditions, unresolved outcomes, and edge-case catalogues.

limitations: The page describes a failure pattern and case evidence; it does not establish that every rare-scenario support problem has the same cause.
